newsitem.title: GERMANY: Telekom sell-off heralds new era for German shares.
newsitem.headline: Telekom sell-off heralds new era for German shares.

text.p: The flotation of German telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom signals the start of a golden age for German equity culture, leading German bankers said at the launch of Telekom's share price on Sunday.

"The private shareholder was pronounced dead many times and now, look, here he is," Ronaldo Schmitz, management board member at Deutsche Bank, said at a press conference to announce the share price for Monday's share issue.

Hansgeorg Hofmann, a board member at Dresdner Bank, which along with Deutsche Bank is one of the global coordinators of the Telekom deal, said: "This is a blockbuster. Considering where we come from, every flotation feels like a new dawn."

Nearly half of the 713 billion shares being issued in Telekom have been allocated to private shareholders, marking a successful conclusion to Telekom's blanket advertising campaign aimed at cultivating interest among small investors.

This figure is higher than expected in a country where only about 5.5 percent of privately-held financial assets are invested in shares, compared with 21 percent in the U.S., where equity investment is a normal part of planning for retirement.

Analysts said the Telekom share issue -- Europe's biggest ever flotation and the second biggest in the world -- shows that further attempts by German banks and companies aimed at developing a equity culture in Germany have been successful.
"If it's a successful privatisation it could get the German market going and help create an equity culture," said Jonathan Shantry, European telecoms analyst at Credit Lyonnais in London.

Germans have more than 3.0 trillion marks ($1,991 billion) in savings and financial institutions have been feverishly wooing investors, especially younger, less risk-averse investors, in the run-up to the Telekom sell-off, encouraging them to get their share of the pie.
German investors traditionally favour fixed income investment options, which are perceived as less risky but do not offer the same potential for high returns.
"If it's a big success it will encourage other German companies to issue more shares," Shantry told Reuters.

One of the main factors behind the renaissance in German share ownership is the fact that with interest rates in Germany and elsewhere at historically low levels, rates of return from bonds and similar products are not what they used to be.

Also, many German companies have been working to introduce the concept of shareholder value by upping levels of transparency and focusing on dividend payments, trying to shed their image as arcane and non-investor friendly.

"Banks are prepared to learn the lesson from the Telekom issue. There are important signs of liquidity in the market and Telekom shows us just what to do to activate this liquidity," said Deutsche Bank's Schmitz.

"There is a desire to create long-term shareholders and there is a need for incentives to keep investors interested. The banks are being invited to understand this issue as a huge opportunity," he added.
The real litmus test for German equity culture, however, will come in the medium term, during which time Telekom will have to perform strongly to provide the returns that investors are looking for.

If the share price and dividend payout does not match the expectations of small investors, many may be hesitant about investing their savings into equities again. -- Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($1=1.5063 Mark)
